When we are dealing with the world of existing things, whether real or ideal, a complete system of axioms is at least conceivable. We may not be able to establish such a system independently of experience, since we can never be sure that the system we have found is genuinely complete. But it is at least possible to imagine one.
With the human or historical world, however, no such system is even conceivable.
The reason is simple: there are no mathematical-style definitions or axioms that apply to human beings.

Because human beings are historical, because their qualities change, there can be no definitions fixed once and for all that establish the properties of a human being. Nor can there be eternal laws or axioms that forever determine how human beings interact with the natural world and with one another.
A philosophical system must be complete. But human beings cannot possibly be fitted into a Spinozist system modeled on geometry.
A completely different, non-mathematical kind of system is therefore required.
Hegel discovered this specifically philosophical kind of system.

We will not examine Hegel’s system in detail here. First, because there will be plenty of opportunity to do so later. Second, because this entire book is itself an example of Hegelian system-building.
But a few things should be said now.
Systems of the Spinozist type take things, whether real or ideal, as their model and are therefore characterized by the absence of time and movement.
Hegel’s system, by contrast, takes human beings as its model and is characterized precisely by the presence of time and movement.

Because human beings are essentially historical, philosophical omniscience must include knowledge of humanity. It must therefore include the history of humanity and, with it, the time in which that history unfolds.

And because human beings have no unchanging qualities given once and for all, but instead exist through constant development and temporal change, a philosophical system must itself have the character of a developing and moving whole.
Omniscience is therefore not complete at the beginning, as it is in Spinoza, in a collection of definitions and axioms presented from the outset.
It coincides instead with the system as a whole and develops gradually as the system itself develops.
Omniscience is not found at the beginning but at the end. It is not the source of the system’s development but its result.

Hegel called this distinctive feature of his system dialectic: its concepts are not given once and for all at the beginning, but gradually develop and emerge from one another, as though reproducing the historical and temporal development of what exists.

Hegel’s system is “realist,” not “idealist,” in the sense that it does not take its concepts from a supposedly self-contained human “reason” independent of the real world, whether natural or historical.
It takes them from the world itself—a world that exists independently of reason and is “revealed” to knowledge only in or through reason.

On the one hand, Hegel’s system necessarily includes knowledge of human history. On the other hand, its logical structure reflects the temporal process of real development and movement within reality itself.
Hegelian realism can therefore be called “historical” or “dialectical”—as Marx, his great disciple, later called his own realism.
Because Hegel’s system is historical and dialectical, it has two important features that we should note here.
First, Hegel does away with the false philosophical idea of “axioms,” or truths that are supposedly self-evident and independent of experience.
No individual proposition within the system is in itself “self-evident.” Some of them can even seem completely implausible when taken on their own.
Only the system as a whole appears true and “self-evident,” because as a whole it corresponds—or ought to correspond—to the real world, meaning both nature and history.
The individual propositions in the system are true only because they are inseparably connected with that whole.
Remove even one proposition and you create a break in the systematic network, destroying the integrity of the system.
So if the system as a whole is true, then the propositions that make it up must also be true, because the system necessarily presupposes all of them together and each of them individually.
An individual proposition is true only insofar as the true system could not exist without it.
It is therefore the complete system—and only the complete system—that guarantees the truth of all its parts.
Second, Hegel’s system guarantees, or is supposed to guarantee, that it is exhaustive.

The system as a whole is meant to show not only that every proposition within it is true, and therefore genuine knowledge, but also that every true proposition whatsoever is contained within the system.
Only in this way can the system genuinely be omniscience.
Hegel achieves this through what he called the “circularity” of his dialectical system.

We begin with some concept—or, better still, with the “simplest” concept, meaning the one with the least content and the greatest generality. This concept reveals some aspect of the real world to consciousness.
Because it serves as our starting point, we call it the “thesis.”
We then subject it to dialectical investigation or “analysis.” In doing so, we see how it necessarily transforms itself into another concept opposed to the first.
This second concept is called the “antithesis.”
Finally, by comparing the thesis dialectically with the antithesis, we discover that the two together form a third concept: the “synthesis.”

This synthesis, which is the result of the dialectical analysis of the first concept, can in turn become the starting point for a new dialectical analysis. It becomes a new thesis, which produces a new antithesis and a new synthesis, and so on.

Now suppose that, after moving forward in this way, we eventually discover that the final synthesis we have reached is nothing other than the original thesis from which the entire dialectical process began.
At that point we know that there is nowhere further to go. We have exhausted all logical possibilities.
To continue would simply mean going through the same path again, and then repeating it forever.
Now suppose that all concepts are dialectically connected with one another and form a single whole.
We must in fact assume this once we reject every form of “mysticism” and say that every concept without exception can be expressed in a single language and within one coherent discourse.

If all concepts are connected dialectically—that is, discursively or “logically”—then once the dialectical circle has closed on itself, we can say that it contains every possible concept and therefore all the knowledge available to a speaking human being.
Human knowledge in its entirety is expressed in a coherent discourse or logos, and nowhere else.
Every meaningful question that can be asked, and every answer that can be given to it—whether true or false—must be expressible within one and the same meaningful discourse.

So if discourse begins from a definite point, develops from that point according to the necessary laws of discourse, both logical and dialectical, and finally returns to its starting point, then we can say that the discourse is exhaustive.
There can be no other discourse outside this one.
Everything that can possibly be said, whether true or false, has already been said within it.
What is expressed by this discourse is therefore genuinely omniscience.

And it is genuine knowledge, because nothing could be raised against it and no room could remain for doubt. Any objection or doubt would itself have to take a discursive, logical form, and every such possibility has already been exhausted within this complete discourse.
We must not think that the system is complete because it is circular.
The reverse is true: it is circular because it is complete.
Its circularity merely reveals its universality; it does not create it.
In other words, before human discourse can be organized into a circular, dialectical system, it must already contain everything that can possibly be expressed in discourse.
Discourse must already reflect, within itself and through itself, everything that exists, whether real or ideal.
For this to be possible, everything that can exist must itself already have actually existed, whether in the present or in the past.
In other words, world history—the process through which ever new possibilities of human existence are realized—must already have reached its end.
A complete and circular system is possible only at the “end of time.”
There is obviously nothing “mystical” hidden in this idea of the “end of history,” which Marx also adopted and which we discussed earlier.
The assumption is simply that humanity will eventually reach the “ideal” stage of social and political life—that is, its genuinely final stage, which, as we know, is communist.
At that point history, in the ordinary sense of the word, will indeed stop.
There will be no more wars, no more revolutions, and no further changes of social or political order.
History will, so to speak, move out of the real world and into history books.

Once humanity has stopped developing in the real historical sense, it will begin, so to speak, to repeat what it has already passed through by “remembering” its past—that is, by studying its completed history.
The circle of real temporal development will thereby be closed, showing that all its possibilities have been exhausted.
Only then will it be possible to exhaust all the possibilities of knowledge and give the complete system of knowledge its circular form.
The appearance of this circular, and therefore complete, knowledge shows us that humanity’s historical development has ended and that human beings have reached their “perfection.”
But history does not end because this knowledge appears.
The reverse is true: this knowledge can appear only because real historical development has already ended.

Hegel himself believed that history had ended in his time. He also claimed that in his Encyclopedia he had in fact produced the circular system of complete knowledge containing absolutely everything that could possibly be known—that is, everything that could be expressed in meaningful discourse.
As we now know, he was mistaken about this.
But that does not count against the correctness of his definition of what a philosophical system of perfect knowledge would have to be.
Such a system really must be circular, because its circularity is the only possible proof of its completeness and truth.
And the system can be circular only if it is dialectical: only if its concepts develop out of one another.
At the same time, because it reflects everything that exists—not only the natural world and the ideal world but also the human world—it must include knowledge of history.
A philosophical system that claims to be circular and complete must therefore be both dialectical and historical.

In other words, if it includes everything that can be thought, it must contain not only every true proposition but also every false one—that is, every proposition humanity has advanced during the course of its history.

More precisely, it is not the isolated propositions within the system that are true. What is true is the system as a whole: precisely the totality of all the errors humanity has made and that together make up its history.
These errors were partial truths mistakenly taken for the whole.
Once integrated into the whole that forms the circular system, they become true. Their combined truth gives us the truth of the system.
If truth consists in reality being “revealed” to knowledge through meaningful discourse, and if the system contains all human discourse, then the system can only be true.
For human discourse, taken in its entirety, can only be the reflection, in its entirety, of the real world.
This complete and circular system necessarily divides into two basic parts.

The first, which Hegel called “Logic,” gives a complete—and therefore circular—description of the “dialectical” movement and development of concepts or “ideas,” in the narrow sense of dialectic: development that is neither spatial nor temporal but logical.
Logic therefore exhausts the ideal world.
The second part gives the complete and circular description of the reality corresponding to these abstract concepts.
On the one hand, this means the spatial or material, “thing-like” counterpart of ideal concepts: their “dialectical” development as the natural world.
Hegel called this section of the second part the “Philosophy of Nature.”
On the other hand, the second part also describes the real, temporal or historical development corresponding to the “dialectical” development described in the first part.
Hegel called this second section of the second part the “Philosophy of Spirit” (when he uses the word “spirit” here, he means the human being).
This historical development ends with the appearance of the very complete and circular system in which that development is described.
The system is therefore circular in one further sense: it contains itself.
Once it reaches its end, there is nothing left to do but travel again along the path already taken, and then repeat it indefinitely.
Let us now sum up what has been said in this chapter.
In the previous chapter, we saw that philosophy necessarily aims at “wisdom”: the ability to answer every question philosophers can ask about themselves.

In this chapter, we have shown that this “wisdom” must necessarily take the form of omniscience, or perfect and absolute knowledge: the ability to give an absolutely satisfactory answer to every meaningful question that can be asked by means of ordinary human discourse or logos.
